note: CJS scoring tables live in the Anthropic sources. JPF imports the CJS band and does not re-author those axes.

references.title: Redeploying Fable 5
used_for: Asks for a shared industry jailbreak-severity standard (section 3).
Names Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and other Glasswing partners as drafters.
Defines jailbreak as a technique that bypasses a model's safeguards; footnote 2 treats bypass as a synonym for that work.
Describes defense in depth: refusal training, classifiers, offline monitoring, and a safety margin that blocks some benign and low-risk dual-use requests.
Classifies reported Fable 5 bypasses to date as minor (safety-margin intrusion), versus narrow harmful and universal jailbreaks.
Proposes four severity axes: capability gain, breadth of capability gain, ease of weaponization, discoverability.
States that the most severe class, if in active use against critical infrastructure, triggers immediate preliminary mitigations, plus 24/7 watch on submission channels.
Analogizes to CVSS for software vulnerabilities (footnote 4).

references.title: More details on Fable 5’s cyber safeguards and our jailbreak framework
used_for: Publishes the draft Cyber Jailbreak Severity (CJS) scale, CJS-0 through CJS-4.
Publishes numeric rubrics for the four axes and the sum-to-band table.
Capability gain of 0 stops scoring; the finding is CJS-0.
The computed band is a floor; it may be raised, never lowered.
Separates high-risk dual use from harm by who is doing the work and under what authorization, then scores the prompt technique without that context.
Puts system-prompt extraction out of CJS cyber scope.
Opens a HackerOne channel for Fable 5 cyber jailbreaks.

references.title: AI Shared Responsibility Framework, V1.0
used_for: Five layers L1 to L5 and eight personas.
Exactly one accountable party per control.
Attestation artifacts per layer.

references.title: AI Incident Response Framework, V1.0
used_for: Lists jailbreaking as an operator incident type under manipulating model behavior.
Keeps prompt injection and indirect prompt injection as separate incident types.
JPF operational class is an input to that intake, not a replacement playbook.

references.title: CoSAI OASIS Open Project Charter
used_for: In scope: securely building, integrating, deploying, and operating AI systems; prompt injection; model theft; poisoning; scaled abuse; inference attacks.
Out of scope: malware generation, phishing generation, misinformation, bias, and other content safety as such.

references.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System
used_for: Base score plus environmental score. CJS as drafted is base plus a temporal-like discoverability axis. JPF supplies the missing environmental modifier for deployed systems.

references.title: Recommendations from the Hugging Face Autonomous Attack
used_for: HITL is not viable for most agentic use cases; hard gates stay on high-impact or irreversible actions, everything else is automatic. Supports ENV hitl_window = 2 as the default for autonomous agents.
Named human owner with pre-authorized shutdown authority. Supports JPF-L1-004.
Instrument the agent (tool use, decision path), not only the network boundary. Supports JPF-L4-003 path attestation.
Distinct non-human identity per agent; no shared account. Supports JPF-L3-001.
Sandbox isolation is untested until tested; the models escaped on the one permitted egress path.
Containment must confirm the agent has stopped acting, not only that it is unreachable. Added to O-2 and above.
Closed-weight models with cyber guardrails refused defender forensics; an open-weight fallback was required. Distinct from CJS scoring of attacker bypasses.

references.title: Who is responsible for what: An accountability assessment of the OpenAI Hugging Face incident
used_for: Production cyber classifiers were off so the lab could measure capability. CJS does not apply when the safeguard being scored is disabled. O is taken from ENV.
Classifier-off evals require a residual-risk statement that names third-party production systems before refusals are removed.

Eval session A wrote objects (Artifactory files, then directory names on WebDAV) that session B could read. That is ENV persistence 2 and a session-isolation miss; JPF-L4-004 only tests tenant A versus tenant B.
SRF layer assignment of the failures: L1 eval policy and incident declaration, L3 harness and untrusted parsers, L4 sandbox isolation and shared caches.
NIST CSF 2.0 does not name agent sessions as an identity class, covert channels on permitted shared services, or classifier-off cyber evals. JPF ENV axes cover those three.
Compensating control when classifiers are off is agent reach: privileges the agent can mint, and systems it can talk to.
